idiom_name: typestate workflow (Request<Pending> -> Request<Approved>) or std::variant, plus an explicit distinct-approver check
implementation_notes: C++ has no enforcement of its own, but two local idioms carry the workflow's structure: the type-state idiom - a request parameterized by its state so that only an approve() call taking a Payment<Pending> can produce the Payment<Approved> that release() accepts - and, since C++17, std::variant<Initiated, Approved, Rejected> with std::visit when the state set is expected to grow. What replaces the classic role structure is the combination of a compile-time state model and a runtime identity check: no type can prove that the approver is a different person, so approver != maker must be an explicit comparison against the authenticated principal at the single choke point, and where the boundary must resist code in the same address space the two duties belong in separate processes with OS credentials (see the C realization). std::optional is sufficient when only 'a second approval exists' must be tracked.
pitfalls: The compiler checks only that the approval step happened, never that it came from a different actor; the identity comparison must be a single, non-bypassable check at the enforcement point.
An approval carried by value is trivially copyable and replayable; bind it to the request identity and revision, or an edited request can be released under an approval given for the old version.
std::variant is C++17; below that floor the state machine is hand-rolled and illegal states become representable again, so the identity check carries the whole rule.
